```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

An FCA calculation has two kernels: one decides how much demand each facility
gathers, the other spreads each facility's supply-to-demand ratio back to
origins. Let demand at cell $i$ be $D_i$, supply at practice $j$ be $S_j$,
and the demand-side and access-side weights be $G_{ij}$ and $H_{ij}$. Then

\[
L_j=\sum_i D_iG_{ij},\qquad R_j=S_j/L_j,\qquad A_i=\sum_j H_{ij}R_j.
\]

This guide rebuilds the E2SFCA surface of [Getting
started](spax-101-intro.html) one step at a time and checks each step against
`spax_e2sfca()`. It uses the same inputs: WorldPop 2020 residents per cell,
GP FTE excluding GPs in training, and travel minutes to each mainland Cornwall
practice. The calculation covers all of mainland Cornwall; the maps zoom in on
the area around Truro so that individual cells stay visible.

```{r inputs}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>                   # mainland only, as in the other guides
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- crop(travel, pop)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)

truro <- ext(-5.30, -4.80, 50.12, 50.42)  # display window only
practices <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()
show <- function(x, title) {
  plot(crop(x, truro), axes = FALSE, main = title,
    col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"))
  points(crop(practices, truro), pch = 3, col = "red")
}
```

## Step 1: decay weights

With Gaussian decay, $W_{ij}=\exp(-d_{ij}^2/2\sigma^2)$, where $d_{ij}$ is the
travel time. We use $\sigma = 10$ minutes, a choice rather than an estimate.
`calc_decay()` works on plain numbers and on rasters alike.

```{r kernel}
minutes <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30)
round(setNames(calc_decay(minutes, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10), minutes), 3)
weights <- calc_decay(travel, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)
show(weights[["L82001"]],
  "Step 1: weight of one Truro practice (L82001), 0 to 1")
```

Each practice has one weight layer. The map shows the layer for a practice in
central Truro (the red crosses are practices): the weight is close to 1 near
it and fades with travel time. The shape follows the travel-time surface, not
straight-line distance; the gaps are estuaries.

## Step 2 (optional): normalize the demand-side weights

The weights of all practices at one cell need not sum to 1. Where many
practices are close, each of them counts the same resident.
`calc_normalize()` offers alternatives: `"standard"` divides each cell's
weights by their sum, and `"semi"` does so only where the sum exceeds 1.

```{r normalize}
row_sum <- function(w) values(sum(w), mat = FALSE)
round(rbind(
  identity = quantile(row_sum(weights), c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
  standard = quantile(row_sum(calc_normalize(weights, "standard")),
    c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
  semi = quantile(row_sum(calc_normalize(weights, "semi")),
    c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
```

In mainland Cornwall the weights at the median cell sum to about 4, and even
the 5th percentile is above 1, so `"standard"` and `"semi"` give almost the
same result here and both differ from `"identity"`. The choice changes the
demand each practice gathers and so the index: normalization is a model
choice, not a correction. In `spax_e2sfca()` the `demand_normalize` argument
applies it to the demand side only. We keep `"identity"`, so $G = H = W$.

## Step 3: gather demand to practices

`gather_weighted()` sums demand times weight over all cells for each practice:
$L_j=\sum_i D_iW_{ij}$. With `simplify = TRUE` it returns a vector named by the
weight layers.

```{r gather}
load <- gather_weighted(pop, weights, simplify = TRUE)
stopifnot(identical(names(load), gp$practice))
```

## Step 4: supply-to-demand ratios

Each practice's ratio is its supply over the demand it gathered, $R_j=S_j/L_j$.
Index supply by the names of `load`, not by position.

```{r ratio}
ratio <- supply[names(load)] / load
near_truro <- c("L82001", "L82028", "L82015", "L82061", "L82045", "L82048")
data.frame(practice = near_truro) |>
  left_join(select(gp, practice, name), by = "practice") |>
  mutate(gp_fte = round(supply[practice], 1),
    weighted_residents = round(load[practice]),
    fte_per_1000 = round(1000 * ratio[practice], 2))
```

The ratios look small because, with identity weights, each resident is
counted by several practices; step 5 adds them back up. The two central Truro
practices share one site, so they gather the same demand.

`spax_e2sfca()` uses a ratio of zero for a practice whose gathered demand is
zero. That is a computational convention, not evidence of anything; with
Gaussian weights every practice here gathers some demand, so it is not used.

## Step 5: spread the ratios back to cells

`spread_weighted()` multiplies each practice's ratio by its weight layer and
sums over practices: $A_i=\sum_j W_{ij}R_j$. It matches values to layers by
position, so pass the ratios in layer order.

```{r spread}
access <- spread_weighted(unname(ratio[names(weights)]), weights)
show(1000 * access, "Step 5: E2SFCA, GP FTE per 1,000 residents")
```

A cell's index is a sum of contributions from every practice. For the cell
containing the central Truro practice, the largest contributions are:

```{r contributions}
cell <- cellFromXY(pop, geom(practices[practices$practice == "L82001", ])[,
  c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE])
w_cell <- unlist(extract(weights, cell))
parts <- sort(1000 * w_cell * ratio[names(w_cell)], decreasing = TRUE)
round(c(head(parts, 5), all_others = sum(parts[-(1:5)]),
  total = sum(parts)), 3)
```

## Check against the packaged functions

The step-by-step surface, the `spax_e2sfca()` wrapper, the more general
`compute_access()` and a plain matrix calculation all agree:

```{r check}
e2sfca <- spax_e2sfca(pop, gp, travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity", id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
general <- compute_access(pop, supply, weights, weights)

W <- values(weights)
D <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
ok <- !is.na(D)
manual <- rep(NA_real_, length(D))
manual[ok] <- drop(W[ok, ] %*% (supply / colSums(W[ok, ] * D[ok])))
for (answer in list(access, e2sfca$accessibility, general)) {
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(values(answer, mat = FALSE), manual,
    tolerance = 1e-10, check.attributes = FALSE)))
}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(drop(load), colSums(W[ok, ] * D[ok]),
  check.attributes = FALSE)))
```

The check verifies this calculation with these inputs; it does not make
different accessibility models equivalent.

## Why the calculation covers the whole mainland

Cropping the inputs to the Truro window before calculating would be quicker,
but every practice, including those outside the window, would then gather only
the demand inside it.

```{r crop-effect}
cropped <- spax_e2sfca(crop(pop, truro), gp, crop(travel, truro),
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity", id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
in_window <- values(crop(e2sfca$accessibility, truro), mat = FALSE)
relative <- values(cropped$accessibility, mat = FALSE) / in_window - 1
round(quantile(100 * relative, c(0, 0.5, 1), na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

These are percentage differences between the cropped and the full calculation
for cells in the window. Every cell's index rises: by about half at the median
and about fifty-fold at the worst cell, on the window's edge, which picks up
practices outside the window whose small remaining demand gives them very high
ratios. Calculate on the full study area and crop
only for display.

## Change the model explicitly

`spax_2sfca()` uses a binary 15-minute catchment for both steps.
`spax_m2sfca()` keeps $W$ on the demand side but uses $W^2$ on the access side.
$W^2$ is below $W$ except at zero travel time, and far below it for distant
practices, so M2SFCA discounts cells whose practices are far away.

```{r alternatives}
twosfca <- spax_2sfca(pop, gp, travel, threshold = 15,
  id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
m2sfca <- spax_m2sfca(pop, gp, travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity", id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
m2_manual <- rep(NA_real_, length(D))
m2_manual[ok] <- drop(W[ok, ]^2 %*% (supply / colSums(W[ok, ] * D[ok])))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(values(m2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE),
  m2_manual, tolerance = 1e-10, check.attributes = FALSE)))
per_1000 <- function(x) 1000 * values(x$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
round(sapply(list(E2SFCA = e2sfca, M2SFCA = m2sfca, `2SFCA` = twosfca),
  function(x) c(quantile(per_1000(x), c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
    resident_weighted = weighted.mean(per_1000(x), D, na.rm = TRUE))), 2)
```

E2SFCA and 2SFCA have the same resident-weighted mean, total supply per
resident, because each uses one kernel for both steps. M2SFCA does not: the
squared access weights are smaller than the demand-side weights, so part of
the supply is not spread back to anyone. None of these indices is a fitted
statistical model. An allocation model instead defines choice probabilities
with an outside option; see [Choosing a model](model-choice.html) and the
[allocation workflow](allocation-workflow.html).
